text:
Prudence had indeed brought all her moral influence to bear upon Marguerite concerning this new life; but Marguerite had replied that she loved me, that she could not live without me, and that, whatever might come of it, she would not give up the happiness of having me constantly beside her, adding that all those whom it displeased were free not to return.

That was what I had heard one day when Prudence had told Marguerite that she had something very important to tell her, and when I had listened at the door of the room in which they had shut themselves away.

Some time later Prudence returned.

I was at the far end of the garden when she came in; she did not see me. From the way Marguerite had gone to meet her, I suspected that a conversation like the one I had already overheard was about to take place again, and I wanted to hear it as I had the other.

The two women shut themselves in a boudoir, and I began listening.

“Well?” asked Marguerite.

“Well! I have seen the duke.”

“What did he say to you?”

“That he willingly forgave you for the first scene, but that he had learned that you were living openly with M. Armand Duval, and that he did not forgive you for that. ‘Let Marguerite leave this young man,’ he told me, ‘and, as in the past, I shall give her everything she wants; otherwise, she must give up asking me for anything whatsoever.’”

“And what did you answer?”

“That I would convey his decision to you, and I promised him that I would make you listen to reason. Think, my dear child, of the position you are losing, and which Armand will never be able to restore to you. He loves you with all his soul, but he does not have enough money to provide for all your needs, and one day he will indeed have to leave you, when it is too late and the duke is no longer willing to do anything for you. Would you like me to speak to Armand?”

Marguerite seemed to be thinking, for she did not answer. My heart was beating violently as I awaited her reply.

“No,” she resumed, “I shall not leave Armand, and I shall not hide in order to live with him. Perhaps it is madness, but I love him! What can you expect? And besides, by now he has grown accustomed to loving me without hindrance; he would suffer too much if he were forced to leave me, even for only an hour a day. Moreover, I do not have so much time left to live that I should make myself unhappy and do the bidding of an old man whose mere sight makes me grow old. Let him keep his money; I shall do without it.”

“But how will you manage?”

“I do not know.”

Prudence was doubtless about to answer something, but I burst in and ran to throw myself at Marguerite’s feet, covering her hands with the tears that the joy of being loved in this way made me shed.

“My life is yours, Marguerite; you no longer need that man—am I not here? Would I ever abandon you, and could I ever pay enough for the happiness you give me? No more constraint, my Marguerite; we love each other! What does the rest matter to us?”

“Oh! Yes, I love you, my Armand!” she murmured, winding both arms around my neck. “I love you as I would not have believed I was capable of loving. We shall be happy, we shall live peacefully, and I shall bid an eternal farewell to this life of which I am now ashamed. You will never reproach me for the past, will you?”

Tears veiled my voice. I could answer only by clasping Marguerite to my heart.

“Very well,” she said, turning back toward Prudence and speaking in an emotional voice, “you will report this scene to the duke, and you will add that we do not need him.”

From that day onward, there was no more talk of the duke. Marguerite was no longer the woman I had known. She avoided everything that might have reminded me of the life amid which I had met her. No wife, no sister ever showed her husband or her brother the love and care that she showed me. That sickly nature was open to every impression, receptive to every feeling. She had broken with her friends as she had with her habits, with her way of speaking as she had with her former expenditures. When people saw us leave the house to go for an outing in a charming little boat I had bought, they would never have believed that this woman, dressed in a white gown, shaded by a large straw hat, and carrying on her arm the simple silk cloak that was to protect her from the coolness of the water, was that same Marguerite Gautier who, four months earlier, had caused a stir with her luxury and her scandals.

Alas! We hastened to be happy, as though we had guessed that we could not be so for long.

For two months we had not even gone to Paris. No one had come to see us except Prudence and that Julie Duprat of whom I have spoken to you, and to whom Marguerite was later to entrust the touching account I have here.

I spent entire days at my mistress’s feet. We opened the windows overlooking the garden, and, watching summer alight joyfully upon the flowers it causes to bloom and beneath the shade of the trees, we breathed side by side that true life which neither Marguerite nor I had understood until then.

This woman displayed a child’s wonder at the smallest things. There were days when she ran through the garden, like a ten-year-old girl, chasing a butterfly or a dragonfly. This courtesan, who had caused more money to be spent on bouquets than would be needed to keep an entire family living happily, would sometimes sit on the lawn for an hour to examine the simple flower whose name she bore.

It was during that time that she so often read Manon Lescaut. Many times I caught her making notes in that book, and she always told me that when a woman loves, she cannot do what Manon did.

Two or three times the duke wrote to her. She recognized the handwriting and gave me the letters without reading them.

Sometimes the wording of those letters brought tears to my eyes.

He had believed that, by closing his purse to Marguerite, he would bring her back to him; but when he had seen how useless that means was, he had been unable to bear it. He had written, asking once again, as in the past, for permission to return, whatever conditions might be imposed upon that return.
